title: How Dark Money Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain dark money in American politics, opening with the 1988 Willie Horton "weekend passes" attack ad funded by the National Security Political Action Committee in support of George H.W. Bush against Michael Dukakis. They trace campaign finance history from Teddy Roosevelt and the Tillman Act, through Watergate and the Nixon CREEP money, to the 501(c)(4) loophole, the 2010 Citizens United v. FEC ruling, and the resulting super PAC spending. They cover disclosure rules, the IRS, SEC and FEC being hobbled, the Koch brothers and climate denial funding, the coordination problem with candidate-released footage, rent seeking, and proposals for public financing. The episode closes with a listener email from coal miner Michael Harrison about job loss in renewable energy transitions.

segments.title: Opening and the Willie Horton ad
segments.summary: Hosts open with the 1988 'Weekend Passes' attack ad on Dukakis, funded by the National Security Political Action Committee, and note the ad's link to the Massachusetts furlough program. They preview dark money and the Supreme Court's role.

segments.title: Super PAC spending statistics and early campaign finance history
segments.summary: Hosts cite that most super PAC money since 2010 came from a small group of wealthy donors. They trace early reform from Teddy Roosevelt and the Tillman Act to Watergate and Nixon's CREEP secret contributions.

segments.title: Loopholes and the 501(c)(4) tax status
segments.summary: They explain that each reform brings a loophole, and describe 501(c)(4) social welfare groups that can accept anonymous donations. They discuss the 1981 IRS rule on primarily social welfare activity.

segments.title: Citizens United v. FEC ruling
segments.summary: The Citizens United case arose from the group's movie ad attacking Hillary Clinton. The Supreme Court ruled for the group, equating money spending with speech and corporations with individuals, and relied on disclosure and regulators to provide transparency.

segments.title: Negative ads, coordination, and partisan dark money
segments.summary: Hosts cite an Annenberg Center finding that most dark money ads in 2012 were negative and many misleading. They discuss candidate-released raw footage used by super PACs and argue Republicans use dark money more than Democrats, with examples involving Bernie Sanders and Hillary Clinton.

segments.title: Money and winning elections, influence and access
segments.summary: Hosts argue that big spenders usually win House and Senate races and that donors gain influence through repeated access even without quid pro quo. They mention Jeb Bush's super PAC spending and the Koch brothers' planned spending for 2016.

segments.title: Comparing countries, IRS and SEC retreat, and FEC deadlock
segments.summary: Hosts discuss whether other wealthy countries face similar problems. They describe the IRS being pressured after targeting tea party groups, Congress riders in an omnibus bill blocking IRS and SEC rules, and the FEC deadlocking along party lines with weakened disclosure of ad spending.

segments.title: Anonymous speech debate and climate change denial funding
segments.summary: They discuss the argument that anonymous political speech is traditional, citing Scalia's dissent on anonymous pamphlets. They describe Robert Brulle's research showing climate denial funding shifted to anonymous 501(c)(4) and foundation channels, and explain rent seeking.

segments.title: Proposed solutions: public financing
segments.summary: Hosts recap the state of dark money and propose strictly public financing of campaigns as a solution, while noting opposition would argue it restricts First Amendment rights. They invite further reading on dark money.

segments.title: Listener mail: coal miners and renewable energy jobs
segments.summary: Listener Michael Harrison, a former underground coal miner, writes about job losses in eastern Kentucky as renewable energy grows. The hosts discuss retraining and government infrastructure investment as responses. The episode closes with a sign-off inviting feedback.
